name: Rhinoceros horn

card.summary: A keratin horn used in some traditional Asian medicine and carving, with claimed cooling and detoxifying effects; its trade is banned and tied to poaching.
card.note: International trade has been banned under CITES since 1977; demand drives poaching.

quick.overview:
Rhino horn is made of keratin, the same protein as human hair and fingernails. In some traditional Asian medicine it has been used for fever and convulsions and for claimed detoxifying effects, and it has also been carved into objects such as dagger handles.

It appears in vitality and wellness discussions, but published sources describe no good evidence of health benefits, and popular aphrodisiac or cancer-cure claims are described as misconceptions. Demand is a driver of poaching.
quick.how: Traditional use is as ground horn in preparations, and consumers in Vietnam and China are described as main users. This entry describes the practice rather than guiding purchase, which is illegal.
quick.risks: International trade has been banned since 1977 and possession and sale are illegal in many places. Poaching has driven rhino population losses. Fake horn is also a concern.

lead: Rhino horn is a keratin structure; traditional medicine has prescribed it for fevers and convulsions and for 'cooling' and detoxifying effects. [1] Wikipedia reports there is no good evidence of benefit, and describes aphrodisiac and cancer-cure beliefs as misconceptions. [1]
Horn has also been carved, and demand for dagger handles in Yemen was a major driver in the 1970s and 1980s. [1] Trade has been banned under CITES since 1977. [1]
Researchers debate whether regulated trade would reduce poaching, while WWF opposes legalisation. [1][2][3] A 2019 study reported creating artificial rhino horns from horse hair. [4]

chain: Horn is ground for traditional preparations
Claimed to cool, detoxify and strengthen
Claimed health and vitality; appearance effect is not documented
angle.text: In traditional medicine it is taken for health claims such as detoxification and fever relief, which some tie to general vitality. No direct appearance effect is documented.

paras: The horn is keratin, as in hair and nails, and has been prescribed in traditional medicine and carved into objects. [1]

South Africa banned domestic sales in 2009, a 2017 court ruling overturned that, and a 2016 proposal to lift the CITES ban was rejected. [1] A 2024 Science Advances study reported poaching pressure on African rhinos at an all-time high. [5] Dehorning was linked to a drop in poaching in a 2025 Science study, per Wikipedia. [1]
